engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

book.author: Chris Voss
book.chapter: Tactical Empathy: The Most Powerful Negotiation Tool
book.lesson: FBI hostage negotiator Chris Voss's core technique: tactical empathy. Not sympathy (feeling what they feel) but empathy (understanding what they feel and why). In any negotiation, the other party has emotional needs underneath their stated position. Label those emotions: 'It seems like you're frustrated by the timeline.' 'It sounds like you feel the value isn't there.' Labelling emotions defuses them and builds trust. When people feel understood, they are more open to creative solutions. The biggest mistake in negotiation is treating it as purely rational — it is almost always emotional first.
book.key_quote: The fastest path to yes in any negotiation is to make the other person feel genuinely understood first.
book.action: In your next difficult conversation, try one label: 'It seems like...' or 'It sounds like...' and see what happens to the tone.
crux: Negotiation is not rational argument. It is emotional intelligence applied under pressure.
Tactical empathy: recognise and name the other side's perspective without agreeing to it.
Mirroring — repeat their last 1–3 words — keeps them talking and reveals information.
Labelling: 'It seems like…', 'It sounds like…'. Naming a negative defuses it.
Run an accusation audit — list their worst assumptions about you and say them first.
'No' is the start of the negotiation, not the end. It creates safety.
Aim for 'That's right', not 'You're right'. The second means they want you to stop.
Never split the difference. Compromise produces outcomes neither side wanted.
Deadlines are usually artificial and almost always work against whoever fears them.
The F-word: fairness. When they invoke it, they feel wronged. Address that, not the maths.
Bend their reality with anchoring, loss aversion, and non-round numbers.
Calibrated 'How' and 'What' questions transfer the problem without confrontation.
'How am I supposed to do that?' is the most useful sentence in the book.
Find the Black Swan — the unknown that reframes the whole deal. Three types of leverage: positive, negative, normative.
learnings: Listening is the tactic, not the courtesy.
Getting to 'no' early saves months of false progress.
Non-round numbers read as calculated; round numbers read as arbitrary.
Compromise is usually mutual loss wearing a diplomatic label.
examples: Voss talked down a Brooklyn bank robber using mirroring alone, with no tactical leverage available.
The Chase Manhattan hostage case: 'It seems like you don't want to go back to jail' opened a conversation that demands had closed.
A student negotiated a salary from $30k to $34k plus a defined promotion path by asking 'How am I supposed to accept that?'
adapt: Dubai salary talk: anchor with a non-round number — AED 32,400, not 30,000. Then ask how they can get there.
Accusation audit before the offer conversation: 'You're probably thinking I'm asking above the band for this level.'
Label the objection about not having UAE experience before they raise it.
Never split the difference on the SIP amount. Automate the number and remove the negotiation with yourself.

interview_tech.q: You acquire 80% of a subsidiary. Walk me through the consolidation mechanics.
interview_tech.a: Recognise 100% of the subsidiary's assets and liabilities at fair value, not 80% — control, not ownership, drives consolidation. The 20% you do not own becomes non-controlling interest, shown within equity. Goodwill is consideration transferred plus NCI measured either at fair value (full goodwill) or at its share of net assets (partial goodwill) — an accounting policy choice that changes the goodwill number materially. Eliminate all intragroup balances, transactions and unrealised profit in stock. Post-acquisition profit splits between parent and NCI by ownership.

interview_tech.q: What is shrinkage, what causes it, and what is an acceptable level?
interview_tech.a: Shrinkage is the gap between book inventory and counted inventory — theft (external and internal), administrative error, damage and supplier short-delivery. Fashion retail typically runs 1–2% of sales; grocery higher. The important split is internal versus external, because the remedies differ entirely: internal is a controls and rostering problem, external is layout, tagging and security. Any store more than 100bps above the estate average is a process failure, not bad luck — investigate the receiving dock first.

interview_soft.q: What do you know about our company?
interview_soft.a: The disqualifying answer is anything from the homepage. Come with: their last reported results and one number from them, their format or brand mix and how it differs from peers, one strategic move in the last 18 months, and one question you genuinely cannot answer from outside. For a Gulf retail group that means knowing their franchise portfolio, which markets they operate directly versus through partners, and their exposure to mall footfall.

interview_soft.q: How do you build credibility in the first 90 days in a new company?
interview_soft.a: Deliver one visible thing early and be accurate about everything. Concretely: get the close done cleanly, learn the actual business by walking the stores rather than reading the reports, and find the one number everyone argues about and fix its definition. Do not restructure anything in the first quarter. Credibility in finance is cumulative and fragile — it comes from being right repeatedly, not from an early bold move.

cfo_field.q: Learn the lease standard properly. In the Gulf it is not a footnote.
cfo_field.a: IFRS 16 put every store lease on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Two consequences a CFO must be able to say out loud: EBITDA is now flattered, because rent that used to sit in operating costs is split into depreciation and interest; and leverage ratios move even though nothing about the business changed. If your covenant is set on a pre-IFRS-16 basis, know it before the bank asks.

cfo_field.q: Automation without a control map is how a finance function loses its audit trail.
cfo_field.a: Before automating a process, write down: who can initiate, who approves, what the system does without a human, and where the exception report goes. Automation does not remove controls; it moves them from people to configuration, and configuration drifts silently. The question 'what breaks if this runs wrong for a month before anyone notices' is the one that separates a finance automation from a finance incident.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece coordination: develop knights before bishops, castle by move 7, and avoid unnecessary queen moves that waste tempo.
lichess_games.standout: 63 moves of grinding. Endgame stamina, not opening prep, settled this one.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece development: avoid moving the same piece twice (e.g., 4...Nf6 → 6...Nxe4). Aim for <15 % time spent on each opening move. Use a basic 3‑move opening plan (develop knights, bishops, castle) to reduce unnecessary pawn pushes and improve positional accuracy.
lichess_games.standout: Finished by checkmate on move 40 — you converted rather than letting it drift.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your 50 % score shows you’re merely treading water—every loss erodes confidence and rating faster than any win can restore it. The fact that you have no recorded upsets or collapses means you’re playing at your current level without ever pushing the envelope; you’re neither threatening higher‑rated opponents nor exploiting weaker ones, which is the hallmark of stagnation. Stop relying on familiar tricks, drill the first 12 moves of at least three solid, theory‑tested openings (e.g., the Caro‑Kann, the London System, and the Slav), and commit to playing each of them in every rapid game for the next 30 days to force deeper preparation and force opponents out of their comfort zones.

lichess_puzzle.tip: Calculate 3 moves deep before touching a piece.
